name: Whole30

image.caption: meeting a friend for dinner, not looking frumpy. I feel weird! haha. also: first dining out experience on #whole30. eeep! it will be hardest to say no to booze.

lead: Whole30 asks participants to eat only whole foods for 30 days, cutting added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and legumes, then to reintroduce them one by one. Its founders frame it as a reset for energy, digestion and cravings. In appearance circles it is used as a short clean-eating protocol for a leaner body and clearer skin.

The chain: removing processed foods and common trigger foods lowers cravings and calorie intake, which people report as a leaner look, and reintroduction is meant to show which foods affect them individually. It was created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. Wikipedia notes no studies had examined its health effects as of 2019.

paras: People follow the strict food list for the full 30 days, plan and cook meals in advance, then bring foods back in one at a time while noting how they feel. The founders discourage weighing and calorie counting during the month.
Dietitians have criticised its restrictiveness and the exclusion of whole grains and legumes. Independent studies on its physical risks are limited.

angle.text: People use Whole30 as a one-month reset, aiming for a leaner body, better energy and clearer skin, then reintroduce foods to spot personal triggers. Cutting processed foods lowers cravings and calories. Gains are mostly reported by users; the program has no controlled trials of its own.

lead: Whole30 is a 30-day elimination diet created in 2009 by Melissa Hartwig (now Melissa Urban) and Dallas Hartwig. For a month, participants eat meat, seafood, eggs, vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds and certain fats and leave out added sugar, alcohol, grains, dairy and (in the original version) legumes and soy, then reintroduce those foods one at a time.[1][2]

People use it as a clean-eating reset aimed at looking and feeling better: less bloat and puffiness, fewer cravings, steadier energy and sleep, and for many a leaner physique and clearer-looking skin. The founders themselves frame it as a reset rather than a weight-loss plan and discourage weighing or calorie counting.[1][2]

On T Nation, lifters mention doing Whole30 alongside lifting plans, for example one poster reporting getting leaner while adding some mass to the delts and upper back, and another planning a month of it with high-rep lifting.[3][4] Wikipedia reports that no studies had specifically examined its health effects as of 2019 and that dietitians are divided on its restrictions.[1]

paras: Allowed foods are meat, seafood, eggs, vegetables, fruit, nuts, seeds and certain fats. It is stricter than the paleo diet because it also bans honey and maple syrup. Participants are told not to count calories or weigh themselves, and the reintroduction phase tests food groups individually [1][2]. A plant-based version permits legumes and soy [1].

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and fitness communities
paras: T Nation posters discuss Whole30 as a version of paleo. One reports doing it with a spouse at moderate carbohydrate intake and getting leaner while adding some mass to the delts and upper back; another plans a one-month Whole30 with a high-rep lifting plan as part of a fat-loss goal.[3][4] A coach on the forum says clients who followed perfect Whole30 or paleo eating got little change when gut health issues were present.[5]

The Hartwigs began the program in April 2009 and co-wrote It Starts with Food (2012) and The Whole30 (2015). They separated in 2015 and Melissa Urban took over the business [1]. A 2016 New York Times article noted over a million Instagram posts using #Whole30, and by 2018 the trademark was licensed to food companies [1]. Grokipedia reports rule updates over time, including allowing white potatoes in 2014 [2].

No studies found. Wikipedia reports that no studies had specifically examined the program's health effects as of 2019.[1] Grokipedia mentions a 2018 pilot study and a survey of completers, which are self-reported and not controlled.[2] A separate modelling study estimated greenhouse gas implications of commercial weight-loss diets, not health effects.[6]

Many dietitians agree with its emphasis on protein, vegetables and avoiding added sugar and alcohol, while some consider it too extreme [1]. David L. Katz criticised excluding whole grains and legumes, saying this conflicts with a large body of evidence [1]. U.S. News and World Report ranked it last of 38 diets in 2016 and 2017, citing restrictiveness and social impact [1].

lore.intro: Followers describe Whole30 as a one-month reset and share results; the founders emphasise non-scale outcomes. On T Nation it is discussed as paleo-style eating alongside training.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Thirty days off sugar, grains, dairy and alcohol resets energy, sleep and cravings.
The reintroduction phase identifies personal food sensitivities.
Excluding legumes and whole grains is necessary.
Strict clean eating produces leaner, better-looking results when paired with training.

timeline.event: Whole30 launched by Melissa and Dallas Hartwig [1][2].
The Whole30 book published; founders separate [1].
Trademark licensed to several food companies [1].
